idiom_name: sealed interface + record cases + exhaustive pattern switch
implementation_notes: Java 17 sealed types (JEP 409) give the closed set - `sealed interface Payment permits Card, Transfer`, with the permits clause inferable when the cases are declared in the same compilation unit - records (JEP 395) give immutable carriers with value equality and accessors, and Java 21 pattern matching for switch (JEP 441) performs a type-coverage check against the permits clause, so a missing case is a compile error with no `default` arm. The check is compile-time only: if the sealed hierarchy gains a permitted subclass and the switch class is not recompiled, the switch throws `MatchException` at run time, so seal and switch must ship together. Use this form whenever the toolchain allows it; the pre-sealed structure stays for Java 8/11 code or when cases need reference identity.
pitfalls: Extending a `permits` list without recompiling the switch turns a previously exhaustive switch into a runtime `MatchException` (JEP 441 / Oracle pattern-matching guide).
Exhaustiveness requires a sealed or enum selector: over an ordinary interface a `default` arm is mandatory and the guarantee is gone.
Record components are final but not deep-immutable: a `List` component can still be mutated unless the constructor makes a defensive copy.
Sealed hierarchies must stay inside one module (or package for the unnamed module); splitting a permitted subclass into another module fails to compile.
Records cannot extend classes, so a case that needs a shared base implementation cannot be a record.

variants.name: Private constructor with final nested cases (pre-sealed Java)
variants.idiom_name: package-private constructor + final immutable subclasses (+ visitor)
variants.implementation_notes: Before Java 17 the closure had to be structural: a private (or package-private) constructor on the abstract base means only the declared subclasses can extend it, each case is `final` with final fields and defensive copies, and elimination is a visitor or an `instanceof` chain ending in a throwing branch. The compiler cannot see the closure, so completeness is verified by tests and review rather than by the build; keep this form for Java 8/11 toolchains or when cases need reference identity, and migrate to sealed types when the platform allows.
pitfalls: No exhaustiveness help: a forgotten case compiles and fails in the throwing branch at run time, or returns a wrong default in a silently mismatched arm.
The private constructor blocks later refactorings (no subclassing from other packages, generated proxies), so the closure is deliberate but binding.
Defensive copies remain the programmer's job: final fields pointing at mutable collections still let a case's payload change after construction.
